chapter_note: This chapter is dominated by late liturgical/institutional application (assent/amen in congregational prayer, sealing, alms, healing, temptation among the elect), with only a small cosmological substrate explaining the divine archetypes (Summons/Obedience as "portals" redeeming the First Man). The editorial fatigue signal matches the text: after the initial cosmological explanation, the chapter drifts into church practice and exempla. A brief Christian/historical notice about "apostles" appears near the end.

paragraphs.temporal_note: Disciple-to-master question formula (hagiographic dialogue frame) with direct address "my master" and request to be taught.

paragraphs.core_text: The assent and the amen have come about from these great ones of the powers. They were given the name as the assent belongs to the summons and the amen belongs to the answer.
paragraphs.removed_material: Removed dialogue attribution frame: "Our enlightener says to him:"
paragraphs.temporal_note: Underlying content is cosmological etiology (assent/amen grounded in "great ones of the powers"; mapped onto Summons/Answer), but introduced by a clear dialogue-frame formula.

paragraphs.core_text: Just as the summons and the obedience are the ones that opened the portals of mercy and entreaty for the First Man, so they also became portals for the Mother of Life and the Father of the living. The First Man sought and found his redeemer. And also the Mother of Life and the Father of the living sought [...] this runner, who came forth from them, who is the First Man; but the summons and the obedience became the portals for them.
paragraphs.temporal_note: Impersonal, process/cosmology exposition: Summons/Obedience as cosmic mechanisms (“portals”) enabling redemption; named cosmic beings (First Man, Mother of Life). No institutional address or moral exhortation.

paragraphs.core_text:
⟨p.293⟩
Now, in this way they have become portals for the aeons of greatness towards the First Man, and the soul that was conjoined with death. They became helpers [...] of the First Man during his ascent. They gave him [...] the Father of Life and the Mother of Life [...]. They are purifiers of the living soul, being helpers and bestowers of remembrance for it, be it either in [...] in the tree or in the creation of flesh [...]
paragraphs.removed_material: Removed the continuation once the paragraph pivots into institutional/application identifications ("the holy church [...] the earth [...]" plus roles like "teacher" and community-focused functions). This section maps the cosmic pattern onto contemporary church structures, indicating an editorial graft.
paragraphs.temporal_note: Opens as continuation of the same cosmological mechanism (portals/helpers/purifiers; ascent; aeons), then shifts into explicit church/institution vocabulary (“holy church”, “teacher”), crossing cosmos→community.
Liturgical instruction about uttering a formula over psalm/prayer and its effect on the blesser; institutional prayer practice rather than cosmic architecture.
Congregational response formula (“verily and amen”) sealing an entreaty; purely church practice.

Direct address (“Happen you know… all of you”), communal benefit language (“came to you profitably”), and daily rebirth motif tied to the congregation; application voice rather than impersonal cosmology.

Mechanism depends on crowds uttering assent/amen; includes explicit institutional virtues (“alms”) and depicts liturgical efficacy (sound sculpting an image). Cosmos-language is harnessed to practice, so the whole paragraph is late application.
Prayer-for-the-sick and bodily danger; practical ritual efficacy rather than systemic cosmological mapping.
Continuation of healing/help motif from assent/amen in applied setting.
Explicit community category (“elect”), moral/temptation counseling, charity request, confession; institutional soteriology and pastoral care.
Applied prayer practice over a person; therapeutic effect language (help/power).
Uses cosmic imagery (“go up to the ships”) but still as a function of the assent/amen uttered in practice; not a standalone cosmological exposition.
Extended applied scenario (danger/enemies/goods/judgement; being saved when assent/amen are called over him). Application-voice density confirms situational exemplum.
Direct address/imperative tone (“Behold… your own cry”), continuing applied exhortation about responding with amen.
Historical/authority anchoring in "apostles" and "first fathers" reflects Christian-heritage overlay and community legitimation rather than the impersonal substrate.
Formulaic closing response (“he glorified…”), characteristic of the redactional frame.
